meta.subject: Mathematics
meta.rendering_note: All mathematical expressions are rendered in KaTeX using \( ... \) delimiters, with one unnested span per expression. Vectors are written as \vec{a}, \vec{AB}, or in component form using \hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k} (never a bare Unicode arrow). Dot products use \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} and cross products use \vec{a}\times\vec{b}, each as a single KaTeX span. No raw Unicode math symbols (·, →, ≤, ≥, ≠, √, π, ∞, ×, ÷, ±) appear outside \( \) delimiters anywhere in the bank.

topics.name: Basic Concepts: Types of Vectors, Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios
topics.summary: A vector has both magnitude and direction, unlike a scalar, which has magnitude only. Key types include the zero vector \(\vec 0\) (zero magnitude, arbitrary direction), unit vectors (magnitude \(1\)), coinitial vectors (same starting point), collinear vectors (parallel to the same line, whether or not they touch), equal vectors (same magnitude and direction regardless of starting point), and the negative of a vector (same magnitude, opposite direction). A position vector locates a point relative to a fixed origin. If a line makes angles \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) with the \(x,y,z\)-axes, \(\cos\alpha,\cos\beta,\cos\gamma\) are its direction cosines \((l,m,n)\), always satisfying \(l^2+m^2+n^2=1\). Any three numbers merely proportional to the direction cosines are direction ratios \((a,b,c)\) — these describe the same direction but are not themselves cosines unless already normalized by dividing each by \(\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}\). This raw-ratio-vs-normalized-cosine distinction is the single most common slip in this topic, and shows up repeatedly whenever direction ratios feed into later calculations.
key_formulas: Unit vector along \(\vec a\): \(\hat a=\dfrac{\vec a}{|\vec a|}\)
topics.worked_example: A vector has direction ratios \((1,2,2)\). Since \(\sqrt{1^2+2^2+2^2}=\sqrt9=3\), its direction cosines are \(\left(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3}\right)\) — not \((1,2,2)\) itself.
common_mistakes: Reporting raw direction ratios directly as direction cosines without dividing by the magnitude \(\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}\)
Forgetting that the negative of a vector reverses all three direction cosines
Confusing 'coinitial' (same starting point) with 'collinear' (parallel to the same line)
Dividing by \(|\vec a|^2\) instead of \(|\vec a|\) when normalizing

topics.name: Addition of Vectors, Multiplication by a Scalar, and the Section Formula
topics.summary: Vectors add by the triangle law (\(\vec{AB}+\vec{BC}=\vec{AC}\)) or, equivalently, the parallelogram law, and vector addition is both commutative and associative, just like ordinary number addition. Multiplying \(\vec a\) by a scalar \(k\) scales its magnitude to \(|k||\vec a|\); the direction stays the same for \(k>0\) and reverses for \(k<0\). Three points \(A,B,C\) are collinear exactly when \(\vec{AB}=k\,\vec{AC}\) for some scalar \(k\) — proportional direction vectors, not necessarily identical ones. The section formula locates the point dividing segment \(AB\) in ratio \(m:n\): internally at \(\dfrac{m\vec b+n\vec a}{m+n}\), and externally at \(\dfrac{m\vec b-n\vec a}{m-n}\); setting \(m=n=1\) in the internal case gives the familiar midpoint formula. These tools combine naturally with the rest of vector algebra — for instance, locating a point via the section formula and then testing its direction cosines, its angle with another vector, or its coplanarity with other points.
key_formulas: Scalar multiplication: \(|k\vec a|=|k||\vec a|\); direction reverses if \(k<0\)
common_mistakes: Using \(\vec a+\vec b\) directly where the midpoint (the average, \(\frac{\vec a+\vec b}{2}\)) was needed
Swapping which ratio number goes with which endpoint in the section formula
Using the internal section formula when the external one was called for, or vice versa
Requiring \(\vec{AB}=\vec{AC}\) exactly for collinearity, instead of the weaker proportionality \(\vec{AB}=k\,\vec{AC}\)

topics.name: Dot Product (Scalar Product): Angle Between Vectors and Projections
topics.summary: The dot product \(\vec a\cdot\vec b=|\vec a||\vec b|\cos\theta\) is a scalar, not a vector, and it's symmetric in its two arguments (\(\vec a\cdot\vec b=\vec b\cdot\vec a\)), unlike the antisymmetric cross product. It's zero exactly when the (nonzero) vectors are perpendicular, and \(\vec a\cdot\vec a=|\vec a|^2\) always. In components, \(\vec a\cdot\vec b=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3\), a simple sum of products. The scalar projection of \(\vec a\) onto \(\vec b\) is \(\dfrac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec b|}\), and the vector projection is that scalar multiplied by \(\hat b\). Because \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec a||\vec b|}\), the dot product is the standard tool for finding angles and testing perpendicularity — and it pairs specifically with cosine, never sine, since sine belongs to the cross product instead. Identities like \(|\vec a+\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2+2\vec a\cdot\vec b+|\vec b|^2\) follow directly from expanding the dot product distributively over vector addition.
key_formulas: Scalar projection of \(\vec a\) on \(\vec b\): \(\dfrac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec b|}\)
\(\vec a\perp\vec b\iff\vec a\cdot\vec b=0\) (for nonzero vectors)
topics.worked_example: For \(\vec a=2\hat i+3\hat j\), \(\vec b=3\hat i-2\hat j\): \(\vec a\cdot\vec b=6-6=0\), so \(\vec a\) and \(\vec b\) are perpendicular.
common_mistakes: Pairing the dot product with \(\sin\theta\) instead of \(\cos\theta\) (that pairing belongs to the cross product)
Reporting the raw dot product as the cosine, forgetting to divide by \(|\vec a||\vec b|\)
Confusing \(\vec a\cdot\vec b=0\) (perpendicular) with \(\vec a=\vec b\) or with parallel vectors
Dividing by only one magnitude instead of both when finding \(\cos\theta\)

topics.name: Cross Product (Vector Product): Area and Direction
topics.summary: The cross product \(\vec a\times\vec b=|\vec a||\vec b|\sin\theta\,\hat n\) is itself a vector, perpendicular to both \(\vec a\) and \(\vec b\), with direction given by the right-hand rule (curl the fingers from \(\vec a\) toward \(\vec b\)). It's antisymmetric: \(\vec b\times\vec a=-(\vec a\times\vec b)\), and \(\vec a\times\vec a=\vec 0\) for any vector. Expanded as a determinant along the top row \(\hat i,\hat j,\hat k\), the cofactor sign pattern is \(+,-,+\) — the \(\hat j\)-term always carries an extra negative sign, the single most common slip in this topic. Geometrically, \(|\vec a\times\vec b|\) is the area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides \(\vec a,\vec b\); halving it gives the corresponding triangle's area. Since \(\sin\theta\) (not \(\cos\theta\)) pairs with the cross product, \(\vec a\times\vec b=\vec 0\) for nonzero vectors means they're parallel, not perpendicular — the opposite of the dot-product condition. Cross products are the standard tool for testing parallelism, building normal vectors, and computing torque (\(\vec r\times\vec F\)) and other angular quantities.
key_formulas: Area of parallelogram \(=|\vec a\times\vec b|\); area of triangle \(=\frac{1}{2}|\vec a\times\vec b|\)
\(\vec a\parallel\vec b\iff\vec a\times\vec b=\vec 0\) (for nonzero vectors)
topics.worked_example: For \(\vec a=\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k\), \(\vec b=4\hat i+5\hat j+6\hat k\): \(\vec a\times\vec b=\hat i(12-15)-\hat j(6-12)+\hat k(5-8)=-3\hat i+6\hat j-3\hat k\).
common_mistakes: Dropping the negative sign in front of the \(\hat j\)-cofactor during the determinant expansion
Pairing the cross product with \(\cos\theta\) instead of \(\sin\theta\)
Computing \(\vec b\times\vec a\) when \(\vec a\times\vec b\) was required, missing the sign flip
Forgetting to halve \(|\vec a\times\vec b|\) when a triangle's (rather than a parallelogram's) area is needed

topics.name: Scalar Triple Product: Coplanarity and Volume
topics.summary: The scalar triple product \([\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)\) is a scalar equal (in magnitude) to the volume of the parallelepiped with coterminous edges \(\vec a,\vec b,\vec c\); the volume of the tetrahedron on the same edges is \(\frac{1}{6}\) of that. Three vectors are coplanar exactly when \([\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=0\) — but this only guarantees coplanarity, not that any two of the vectors are parallel or equal. The triple product is unchanged under a cyclic permutation of its three vectors (\([\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=[\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec a]=[\vec c\ \vec a\ \vec b]\)), but a single swap of any two vectors flips its sign — the central trap in this topic. It's also linear in each argument, so scaling one vector by \(k\) scales the whole triple product by \(k\), and a repeated vector always forces the triple product to zero.
key_formulas: \([\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)\)
Volume of parallelepiped \(=|[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]|\)
Volume of tetrahedron \(=\dfrac{1}{6}|[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]|\)
Coplanarity: \(\vec a,\vec b,\vec c\) coplanar \(\iff[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=0\)
Cyclic invariance: \([\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=[\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec a]\); single swap: \([\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=-[\vec b\ \vec a\ \vec c]\)
topics.worked_example: For \(\vec a=2\hat i\), \(\vec b=3\hat j\), \(\vec c=4\hat k\): \([\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=2\times3\times4=24\), the volume of the box with these mutually perpendicular edges.
common_mistakes: Reporting the raw (possibly negative) scalar triple product as the volume, forgetting the absolute value
Treating a single swap of two vectors as sign-preserving, or a cyclic permutation as sign-flipping (they're the reverse)
Using the parallelepiped's volume formula for a tetrahedron (or vice versa), missing the factor of \(\frac{1}{6}\)
Over-interpreting \([\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=0\) as forcing the vectors to be pairwise parallel or equal, rather than just coplanar

questions.topic: Basic Concepts: Types of Vectors, Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios
questions.question: Which of the following best defines a unit vector?
options: A vector that points along the positive \(x\)-axis only
A vector whose direction ratios are all equal
questions.explanation:
A unit vector is defined purely by its magnitude, not by its direction.

A vector \(\vec{a}\) is called a unit vector when \(|\vec{a}|=1\), regardless of which direction it points in.
questions.hint: Think about which single property of a vector, not its direction, makes it a unit vector.
distractor_logic: confuses the definition of a unit vector with that of a zero vector
wrongly restricts unit vectors to a single fixed direction, when any direction is allowed as long as the magnitude is \(1\)
invents an unrelated condition on direction ratios that has nothing to do with magnitude

questions.topic: Basic Concepts: Types of Vectors, Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios
questions.question: The zero vector \(\vec{0}\) is the vector whose
options: magnitude is \(1\) and whose direction is not defined
magnitude is \(0\) and whose direction is not defined
magnitude is \(0\) and whose direction is along the \(x\)-axis
questions.explanation:
The zero vector \(\vec{0}\) has magnitude \(0\).

Since a direction can only be assigned to a vector with nonzero length, the zero vector's direction is left undefined (or is considered arbitrary).
questions.hint: A vector needs some length to point somewhere; think about what happens when that length is zero.
distractor_logic: mixes up the zero vector's magnitude with that of a unit vector
wrongly assigns a fixed direction to the zero vector, which by definition has no specific direction
describes a vector with unit components, not a vector of zero magnitude

questions.topic: Basic Concepts: Types of Vectors, Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios
questions.question: Two vectors \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) are said to be equal vectors when
options: they have the same magnitude, regardless of direction
they have the same initial point
they have the same magnitude and the same direction
they are parallel to the same line, regardless of magnitude
questions.explanation:
Vector equality requires both conditions together: \(\vec{a}=\vec{b}\) only when \(|\vec{a}|=|\vec{b}|\) and \(\vec{a}\), \(\vec{b}\) point in the same direction.

Matching only magnitude, or only direction (as with collinear vectors), is not enough.
questions.hint: Two conditions must hold together for vectors to be equal, not just one of them.
distractor_logic: drops the direction requirement, so it would also call two same-magnitude vectors pointing in different directions equal
confuses equality of vectors with the unrelated notion of coinitial vectors, which only share a starting point
confuses equality with collinearity, which only requires parallel supporting lines and says nothing about magnitude

questions.topic: Basic Concepts: Types of Vectors, Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios
questions.question: The direction cosines of a vector directed along the positive \(y\)-axis are
questions.explanation:
A vector along the positive \(y\)-axis makes angles \(90°,0°,90°\) with the \(x,y,z\) axes respectively.

Its direction cosines are therefore \((\cos90°,\cos0°,\cos90°)=(0,1,0)\).
questions.hint: Work out the angle this vector makes with each of the three axes separately, then take cosines.
distractor_logic: gives the direction cosines of the positive \(x\)-axis instead of the \(y\)-axis
flips the sign, giving the direction cosines of the negative \(y\)-axis instead
uses an un-normalized pair of ratios rather than the actual direction cosines of a single axis

questions.topic: Basic Concepts: Types of Vectors, Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios
questions.question: For any vector in space, its direction cosines \(l,m,n\) always satisfy
questions.explanation:
If a vector makes angles \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) with the \(x,y,z\) axes, its direction cosines are \(l=\cos\alpha, m=\cos\beta, n=\cos\gamma\).

These always satisfy \(l^2+m^2+n^2=1\), which follows from the vector's magnitude being consistent along all three axes.
questions.hint: Recall the one fixed identity that every valid direction-cosine triple must obey.
distractor_logic: replaces the correct sum-of-squares identity with a simple linear sum, a common but incorrect shortcut
sets the sum of squares to \(0\) instead of \(1\), which would force every direction cosine to vanish
invents a product-based identity that direction cosines have no reason to satisfy

questions.topic: Basic Concepts: Types of Vectors, Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios
questions.question: If \(P(x,y,z)\) is a point in space and \(O\) is the origin, the position vector of \(P\) is
questions.explanation:
The position vector \(\vec{OP}\) of a point \(P(x,y,z)\) is simply the vector from the origin \(O\) to \(P\).

Its components are exactly the coordinates of \(P\), so \(\vec{OP}=x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}\).
questions.hint: A position vector's components are just the point's coordinates, with no extra scaling.
distractor_logic: normalizes the position vector into a unit vector instead of leaving it as \(\vec{OP}\) itself
swaps the \(x\) and \(y\) components when writing the vector
collapses the three coordinates into a single sum multiplying a fixed direction, which is not how a position vector is built

questions.topic: Basic Concepts: Types of Vectors, Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios
questions.question: Vectors \(\vec{AB}\) and \(\vec{CD}\) are called collinear vectors when
options: they have the same initial point \(A=C\)
they have exactly the same magnitude
they lie along the same line or along parallel lines
the angle between them is always \(90°\)
questions.explanation:
Collinear vectors are vectors whose supporting lines are the same line or are parallel to each other, irrespective of their magnitudes or initial points.

They can point in the same direction or in opposite directions, as long as the lines they lie along are parallel.
questions.hint: Focus on the line each vector lies along, not on where it starts or how long it is.
distractor_logic: confuses collinearity, a condition about the supporting lines, with coinitial vectors, a condition about the starting point
brings in magnitude, which plays no role in whether two vectors are collinear
describes perpendicular vectors, the opposite geometric relationship to collinear (parallel) vectors

questions.topic: Basic Concepts: Types of Vectors, Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios
questions.question: Negative of a vector \(\vec{a}\) is a vector that has
options: the opposite magnitude and the same direction as \(\vec{a}\)
half the magnitude of \(\vec{a}\) and the opposite direction
the same magnitude and the same direction as \(\vec{a}\)
the same magnitude as \(\vec{a}\) but the opposite direction
questions.explanation:
\(-\vec{a}\) is defined to have the same magnitude as \(\vec{a}\), i.e. \(|-\vec{a}|=|\vec{a}|\), but it points in exactly the opposite direction.

Magnitude itself can never be negative, so only the direction flips.
questions.hint: Magnitude can never be negative; think about which property actually flips when a vector is negated.
distractor_logic: tries to negate the magnitude itself, which is impossible since magnitude is always non-negative, while leaving the direction unchanged
introduces an unwarranted halving of magnitude that has nothing to do with negating a vector
describes \(\vec{a}\) itself rather than its negative, since both magnitude and direction are left unchanged

questions.topic: Addition of Vectors, Multiplication by a Scalar, and the Section Formula
questions.question: According to the triangle law of vector addition, if \(\vec{AB}\) and \(\vec{BC}\) represent two sides of a triangle taken in order, the third side represents
questions.explanation:
The triangle law states that if two sides of a triangle, taken in order, represent \(\vec{AB}\) and \(\vec{BC}\), then the third side taken in the reverse order represents their sum.

So \(\vec{AB}+\vec{BC}=\vec{AC}\), going from the start point \(A\) to the end point \(C\).
questions.hint: Trace the path from the very first point to the very last point of the two vectors added in order.
distractor_logic: reverses the direction of the resultant, giving \(\vec{CA}\) instead of \(\vec{AC}\)
uses subtraction in place of addition, which the triangle law does not call for
names the wrong side of the triangle entirely, giving \(\vec{BA}\)

questions.topic: Addition of Vectors, Multiplication by a Scalar, and the Section Formula
questions.question: Vector addition is commutative, meaning that for any two vectors \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\),
questions.explanation:
Commutativity of vector addition means the order in which two vectors are added does not matter.

So \(\vec{a}+\vec{b}=\vec{b}+\vec{a}\), with both sides remaining vectors (not magnitudes) and both remaining sums (not differences).
questions.hint: Commutativity only swaps the order of the two vectors being added — nothing else changes.
distractor_logic: turns addition into subtraction on the right-hand side, which is not what commutativity states
confuses the vector sum \(\vec a+\vec b\) with the scalar sum of their magnitudes \(|\vec a|+|\vec b|\)
reverses the order and also switches to subtraction, doing two things wrong at once

questions.topic: Addition of Vectors, Multiplication by a Scalar, and the Section Formula
questions.question: If \(k\) is a scalar and \(\vec{a}\) is a vector, the magnitude of \(k\vec{a}\) is
questions.explanation:
Scaling a vector by \(k\) scales its length by \(|k|\), since magnitude must stay non-negative regardless of the sign of \(k\).

So \(|k\vec{a}|=|k|\,|\vec{a}|\), never \(k|\vec{a}|\) directly (which could go negative).
questions.hint: Magnitude can never be negative, so think about what needs to happen to \(k\) before it multiplies \(|\vec{a}|\).
distractor_logic: drops the absolute value on \(k\), which breaks down whenever \(k\) is negative since a magnitude can never be negative
squares the scalar unnecessarily instead of just taking its absolute value
squares the vector's magnitude instead of the scalar

questions.topic: Addition of Vectors, Multiplication by a Scalar, and the Section Formula
questions.question: If \(k<0\), the vector \(k\vec{a}\) (for nonzero \(\vec{a}\)) points
questions.explanation:
Multiplying \(\vec{a}\) by a scalar \(k\) only changes its magnitude by \(|k|\) and, when \(k\) is negative, reverses its direction.

This reversal happens for any negative \(k\), regardless of whether \(|k|\) is bigger or smaller than \(1\).
questions.hint: It is the sign of \(k\), not its size, that decides whether the direction flips.
distractor_logic: ignores the effect of the negative sign entirely, as though scalar multiplication by a negative number left direction unchanged
introduces perpendicularity, which scalar multiplication (as opposed to some other operation) never produces
wrongly makes the direction-reversal depend on the size of \(|k|\), when it is only the sign of \(k\) that matters

questions.topic: Addition of Vectors, Multiplication by a Scalar, and the Section Formula
questions.question: By the parallelogram law, if \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) are represented by two adjacent sides of a parallelogram drawn from the same point, their sum \(\vec{a}+\vec{b}\) is represented by
options: the diagonal of the parallelogram through their common initial point
the other diagonal of the parallelogram
the side of the parallelogram parallel to \(\vec{a}\)
questions.explanation:
In the parallelogram law, \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) are drawn as adjacent sides from a common point.

Their sum \(\vec{a}+\vec{b}\) is then represented by the diagonal of the parallelogram that starts from that same common point, not by the other diagonal or by either side alone.
questions.hint: Focus on which diagonal shares its starting point with both \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\).
distractor_logic: picks the diagonal that represents \(\vec{a}-\vec{b}\) (or \(\vec b - \vec a\)) instead of the one representing the sum
confuses the resultant diagonal with one of the original sides used to build the parallelogram
treats the entire perimeter as representing the sum, which is not a single vector at all

questions.topic: Addition of Vectors, Multiplication by a Scalar, and the Section Formula
questions.question: The position vector of the midpoint \(M\) of segment \(AB\), where \(A\) and \(B\) have position vectors \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\), is
questions.explanation:
The midpoint of \(AB\) is the average of the two position vectors: \(\vec{m}=\dfrac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}}{2}\).

Both the averaging (division by \(2\)) and the addition (rather than subtraction) are essential parts of this formula.
questions.hint: A midpoint is an average of two positions — think about what operation 'average' involves.
distractor_logic: forgets to divide by \(2\), so this would land at twice the midpoint's actual position
uses subtraction in place of addition, which produces a vector related to displacement, not the midpoint
uses subtraction with the terms in the opposite order, changing the sign but keeping the same underlying error

questions.topic: Addition of Vectors, Multiplication by a Scalar, and the Section Formula
questions.question: The vector \(\vec{a}-\vec{b}\) can be written as
questions.explanation:
Subtracting a vector is the same as adding its negative.

So \(\vec{a}-\vec{b}=\vec{a}+(-\vec{b})\), where only \(\vec{b}\) is negated and \(\vec{a}\) is left untouched.
questions.hint: Only the vector being subtracted gets negated; the other vector stays exactly as it is.
distractor_logic: negates \(\vec{a}\) instead of \(\vec{b}\), which actually produces \(\vec{b}-\vec{a}\), the negative of what was asked
negates the entire sum \(\vec a+\vec b\) rather than just \(\vec b\), which is a completely different vector
negates both vectors instead of just \(\vec b\), giving \(-\vec a-\vec b\) rather than \(\vec a-\vec b\)

questions.topic: Addition of Vectors, Multiplication by a Scalar, and the Section Formula
questions.question: By the section formula, if a point \(R\) divides the join of \(A(\vec{a})\) and \(B(\vec{b})\) internally in the ratio \(m:n\), the position vector of \(R\) is
questions.explanation:
For internal division in the ratio \(m:n\) (measured as \(AR:RB=m:n\)), the point nearer \(B\)'s side gets weight \(m\) and the point nearer \(A\)'s side gets weight \(n\): \(\vec{r}=\dfrac{m\vec{b}+n\vec{a}}{m+n}\).

Mixing up which weight goes with which point, or switching to a minus sign in the denominator, changes the formula into something else entirely.
questions.hint: The weight \(m\) (from the ratio \(AR:RB\)) attaches to \(\vec b\), and \(n\) attaches to \(\vec a\) — and the denominator is a sum, not a difference, for internal division.
distractor_logic: swaps which position vector is paired with which weight, attaching \(m\) to \(\vec{a}\) and \(n\) to \(\vec{b}\) instead of the other way around
changes internal division into external division by using \(m-n\) in the denominator, on top of leaving the weights unswapped
keeps the weights unswapped and additionally uses the external-division denominator \(m-n\) instead of \(m+n\)

questions.topic: Dot Product (Scalar Product): Angle Between Vectors and Projections
questions.question: The dot product (scalar product) of two vectors \(\vec a\) and \(\vec b\) is defined as
options: \(\vec a\cdot\vec b=|\vec a||\vec b|\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between them
questions.explanation:
The dot product of two vectors is a scalar, computed as the product of their magnitudes and the cosine of the angle between them: \(\vec a\cdot\vec b=|\vec a||\vec b|\cos\theta\).

This is the defining formula that connects the dot product to angle.
questions.hint: Remember that it is cosine, not sine, that pairs with the dot product.
distractor_logic: pairs the dot product with \(\sin\theta\), which is actually the trigonometric ratio associated with the cross product, not the dot product
adds the magnitudes instead of multiplying them before bringing in \(\cos\theta\)
drops the angle dependence entirely, as though the dot product never changed with direction

questions.topic: Dot Product (Scalar Product): Angle Between Vectors and Projections
questions.question: If \(\vec a\cdot\vec b=0\) for two nonzero vectors, then \(\vec a\) and \(\vec b\) are
options: collinear but pointing in opposite directions
questions.explanation:
Since \(\vec a\cdot\vec b=|\vec a||\vec b|\cos\theta\), and \(|\vec a|,|\vec b|\) are nonzero, \(\vec a\cdot\vec b=0\) forces \(\cos\theta=0\), i.e. \(\theta=90°\).

So \(\vec a\) and \(\vec b\) must be perpendicular.
questions.hint: Think about which angle makes \(\cos\theta\) equal to zero.
distractor_logic: describes parallel vectors, which would actually make \(|\vec a\cdot\vec b|\) as large as possible, not zero
confuses a zero dot product with vector equality, two unrelated conditions
describes anti-parallel (collinear, opposite-direction) vectors, which also give a nonzero (negative) dot product, not zero

questions.topic: Dot Product (Scalar Product): Angle Between Vectors and Projections
questions.question: The dot product satisfies the commutative property, meaning
questions.explanation:
Commutativity of the dot product means \(\vec a\cdot\vec b=\vec b\cdot\vec a\), following directly from \(|\vec a||\vec b|\cos\theta\) being symmetric in \(\vec a\) and \(\vec b\).

This is different from the cross product, which flips sign when the order is reversed.
questions.hint: The dot product behaves like ordinary multiplication when it comes to order — unlike the cross product.
distractor_logic: states the antisymmetry property of the cross product (\(\vec a\times\vec b=-\vec b\times\vec a\)) as though it applied to the dot product instead
confuses the dot product with the cross product, which produces a vector rather than a scalar
wraps the dot product in an absolute value for no reason, which is not what commutativity means

questions.topic: Dot Product (Scalar Product): Angle Between Vectors and Projections
questions.question: For any vector \(\vec a\), the dot product \(\vec a\cdot\vec a\) equals
questions.explanation: Since the angle between \(\vec a\) and itself is \(0°\), \(\vec a\cdot\vec a=|\vec a||\vec a|\cos0°=|\vec a|^2\).
questions.hint: Apply the definition \(\vec a\cdot\vec b=|\vec a||\vec b|\cos\theta\) with \(\vec b=\vec a\) and \(\theta=0°\).
distractor_logic: forgets to square the magnitude, reporting \(|\vec a|\) itself
wrongly assumes a vector dotted with itself must vanish, when it actually equals its own squared magnitude

The triangle's area is \(\frac{1}{2}|\vec a||\vec b|\sin\theta=\frac{1}{2}\times5\times10\times\sin30°\).

questions.question: \(P\) divides \(A(0,0,0)\) and \(B(6,0,0)\) internally in ratio \(1:2\), and \(Q(0,4,0)\) is another point. Find \(\cos\theta\), where \(\theta=\angle QPO\) (the angle at \(P\) between \(\vec{PQ}\) and \(\vec{PO}\)).
questions.explanation:
\(P=(2,0,0)\) by the section formula. From the vertex \(P\): \(\vec{PO}=-2\hat i\) and \(\vec{PQ}=-2\hat i+4\hat j\).

\(\cos\theta=\dfrac{\vec{PO}\cdot\vec{PQ}}{|\vec{PO}||\vec{PQ}|}=\dfrac{4}{2\times2\sqrt5}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\).
questions.hint: First locate \(P\) via the section formula, then be careful to build both vectors starting FROM the vertex \(P\).

\(\vec R=\vec F_1+\vec F_2=3\hat i+4\hat j\), so \(|\vec R|=5\).

\(\cos\theta=\dfrac{\vec R\cdot\vec c}{|\vec R||\vec c|}=\dfrac{3}{5}\), so \(\sin\theta=\dfrac{4}{5}\); the triangle's area is \(\frac{1}{2}\times5\times1\times\dfrac{4}{5}=2\) square units.

By the internal section formula, \(P=\dfrac{1\cdot(0,0,6)+2\cdot(0,0,0)}{3}=(0,0,2)\), so \(\vec{OP}=2\hat k\).

\([\vec{OQ}\ \vec{OR}\ \vec{OP}]=12\), so the tetrahedron's volume is \(\frac{1}{6}\times12=2\) cubic units.

options: It depends on the specific components of \(\vec{OA}\) and \(\vec{OB}\) — it isn't always \(0\)
It cannot be determined without knowing \(\vec{OA}\times\vec{OB}\) explicitly
\(0\), since \(\vec{OC}\) is a linear combination of \(\vec{OA}\) and \(\vec{OB}\), so all three automatically lie in the same plane
questions.explanation:
Since \(\vec{OC}=\vec{OA}+\vec{OB}\), \([\vec{OA}\ \vec{OB}\ \vec{OC}]=[\vec{OA}\ \vec{OB}\ \vec{OA}]+[\vec{OA}\ \vec{OB}\ \vec{OB}]\).

Each of these two triple products is automatically \(0\) (a triple product with a repeated vector is always \(0\)), so \([\vec{OA}\ \vec{OB}\ \vec{OC}]=0\) — the diagonal of a parallelogram always lies in the same plane as its two adjacent sides.

questions.question: If \(\vec a\times\vec b=3\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k\) and \(\vec c=2\hat i+\hat j-\hat k\), find \([\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]\).
options: \(3\), but only because \(\vec a\cdot\vec b\) happens to equal \(0\) in this case
\(3\), and \(\vec a\cdot\vec b\) plays no role in this calculation at all
This cannot be found without knowing \(\vec a\) and \(\vec b\) individually, not just \(\vec a\times\vec b\)
questions.explanation:
By the cyclic property, \([\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=[\vec c\ \vec a\ \vec b]=\vec c\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)\).

So \([\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=(2)(3)+(1)(-1)+(-1)(2)=6-1-2=3\); this calculation only ever used \(\vec a\times\vec b\) as a single combined vector, so \(\vec a\cdot\vec b\) plays no role at all.
questions.hint: Use \([\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=\vec c\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)\) directly — you don't need \(\vec a\) and \(\vec b\) individually once you already have \(\vec a\times\vec b\).
